We are developing an Ayurvedic wound-care gel in India. Our employee created the extraction process during paid work, a university laboratory optimized stability under a collaboration agreement, and a freelance designer made our label. At a trade fair six months ago we publicly showed the gel and handed out a leaflet naming the ingredients, but we did not disclose extraction temperatures or ratios. We now want to patent the process, keep remaining know-how confidential, register the name and protect the packaging.

Before proposing a strategy, identify the facts that could change ownership or patentability and explain why each matters. Distinguish inventorship from ownership, patentability from freedom to operate, prior public disclosure from remaining secrecy, and artwork copyright from functional packaging design. Do not assume the company owns the university work. Give conditional outcomes and exact Indian statutory citations. Explicitly mark any point the corpus cannot support.

citations.title: Confidential know-how and limits of trade-secret protection
citations.snippet: The WIPO India overview (June 2024) reports protection of confidential formulae and technical know-how through contracts (including NDAs and employment confidentiality clauses) and common-law breach of confidence. The information itself must be confidential; publicly known processes do not qualify merely because a contract labels them secret. Protection depends on the facts and obligations of confidence and generally does not prevent reverse engineering through a confidentiality clause. This is an official intergovernmental overview, not an enacted Indian trade-secret statute; it reports no separate exclusive trade-secret statute at that date. A practical strategy is access controls and documented confidentiality obligations for genuinely secret process know-how, assessed alongside patent disclosure and mandatory drug labels. Current law and enforceability of particular restrictions need professional confirmation.

citations.title: Patent disclosure and biological source/origin
citations.snippet: A complete specification must fully and particularly describe the invention and its operation or use and method of performance, disclose the best method known to the applicant for which protection is claimed, and define the scope through claims. Required enabling details and the best method cannot simply be withheld from a patent specification as trade secrets.

prompt: We plan an Ayurvedic oral syrup containing vasaka and tulsi. India label: 'Ayurvedic proprietary medicine'; Germany label: 'traditional herbal medicine'; US label: 'dietary supplement'. Our website will say 'cures bronchitis'. All herbs are cultivated in India and bought from traders; our company has a German majority shareholder. We have not fixed dosage, proved a history of medicinal use in Europe, or checked US ingredient notification history. Give a separate India/Germany/US decision path for classification, claims and the key evidence or permissions needed. Explain whether cultivated sourcing by itself settles Indian biodiversity and benefit-sharing questions. Identify what cannot yet be concluded; do not treat the three proposed labels as approved classifications.

**Facts still needed and conditional outcomes**

- **What are the complete ingredients and quantities, their authoritative-text references, the exact formula, dosage form, route and intended claims? Studying classical texts alone does not supply those details.** Inference/application: If the complete formulation and manufacture match a First-Schedule authoritative formula, assess the classical route; if they do not, that classical test is not met (s.3(a)) [dc_3a] A non-classical formulation may fit the proprietary route only if all ingredients meet its book-based test and administration is non-parenteral; neither a new brand nor company development establishes this (s.3(h)(i)) [dc_3h]
- **What evidence verifies the stated ownership/control and establishes the actual applicant's statutory category?** Inference/application: You supplied these applicant/entity assertions: “All herbs are cultivated in India and bought from traders; our company has a German majority shareholder.” Verify the actual applicant's incorporation and control, and citizenship/residence where applicable, against section 3(2). Stated Indian ownership or a foreign shareholder alone does not settle that statutory category. Apply prior NBA approval only to the covered applicant and access purpose; company share ownership does not determine ownership of IP. (ss.3(1)-(2); amendment s.5; Biological Diversity Rules, 2024 r.13) [bda_s3] If the applicant falls within section 3(2), assess prior NBA approval for covered access; an Indian manufacturing address does not settle citizenship, residence or foreign control (ss.3(1)-(2); amendment s.5; Biological Diversity Rules, 2024 r.13) [bda_s3] For a person outside section 3(2), assess section 7 prior SBB intimation and its actual exemptions for covered commercial access (s.7(1) proviso, s.7(2)-(3); Amendment Act s.9, p.4) [bda_s7_exemption] The same applicant distinction changes the IP milestone: NBA approval before grant for section 3(2) persons, versus pre-grant registration and applicable commercialisation approval for section 7 persons (s.6(1), s.6(1A), s.6(1B); Amendment Act s.8, pp.3-4) [bda_s6]

**Classical or proprietary medicine**

Established by source: The classical ASU definition requires manufacture exclusively according to formulae in the authoritative books listed in the First Schedule. (s.3(a)) [dc_3a] An ASU patent or proprietary medicine must contain only ingredients mentioned in formulae in First-Schedule authoritative books; the formulation itself must not be included there, and parenteral medicines are excluded. (s.3(h)(i)) [dc_3h]

Inference/application: Classical status remains unresolved: compare the complete formula and manufacture with a First-Schedule formula. Developing a combination yourself or studying classical texts does not establish either a match or its absence. [dc_3a] The proprietary category is conditional on every ingredient meeting the First-Schedule book test, the formulation itself being absent from those formulae, and a non-parenteral route. Calling the product new or proprietary does not verify those facts or establish patentability. [dc_3h]

Not established by retrieved sources: The exact formula and its comparison with the relevant authoritative books have not been verified. The supplied product ingredients or route are unverified. The complete ingredient list, ingredient-by-ingredient authoritative-book references, formulation comparison and exact administration route must establish every condition of this definition.

**Biodiversity access: section 3 and applicant status**

Established by source: Section 3 requires prior NBA approval for the specified access purposes by persons within s.3(2), which distinguishes non-citizens, the specified non-resident citizens and covered foreign/foreign-controlled entities. (ss.3(1)-(2); amendment s.5; Biological Diversity Rules, 2024 r.13) [bda_s3] The Biological Diversity Act defines biological resources and commercial utilisation and includes specific exclusions; applicability depends on the resource, associated knowledge and activity. (ss.2(a), 2(c), 2(ea), 2(f), 2(fa), 2(p)) [bda_scope]

Inference/application: You supplied these applicant/entity assertions: “All herbs are cultivated in India and bought from traders; our company has a German majority shareholder.” Verify the actual applicant's incorporation and control, and citizenship/residence where applicable, against section 3(2). Stated Indian ownership or a foreign shareholder alone does not settle that statutory category. Apply prior NBA approval only to the covered applicant and access purpose; company share ownership does not determine ownership of IP. [bda_s3] The Indian identity or name of a plant alone does not settle the access route. The material's actual source and whether the accessed item falls within the statutory definitions matter. [bda_scope]

Not established by retrieved sources: Ownership/control assertions have been supplied but not verified. Confirm the actual applicant and documentary incorporation/control or citizenship/residence details, the access purpose and the material, before deciding the statutory applicant category. Actual sourcing, material type, date/purpose of access and any relevant exemption remain to be verified.

**Biodiversity duties for IP: section 6**

Established by source: For IP based on research/information on a biological resource accessed from India (including deposits in repositories outside India), or associated traditional knowledge, s.6(1) requires s.3(2) persons to obtain NBA approval before grant. Section 6(1A) requires NBA registration by s.7 persons before grant; under s.6(1B), those s.7 persons obtaining the IP right need prior NBA approval at commercialisation. (s.6(1), s.6(1A), s.6(1B); Amendment Act s.8, pp.3-4) [bda_s6] Rule 16 of the 2024 Rules prescribes Form 7 for s.3(2) IP approval, Form 8 for s.7 pre-grant registration and Form 9 for s.7 commercialisation approval. Rule 18 prescribes Form 10 for the covered use in India of resources or associated knowledge obtained from a foreign country. (G.S.R.665(E), 22 October2024; rr.16,18; Forms7-10) [bda_ipr_forms]

Inference/application: If the IP is based on the covered Indian-accessed resource or associated knowledge, identify the applicant category: section 3(2) persons need NBA approval before grant; section 7 persons need NBA registration before grant and, if they obtain the IP right, prior NBA approval at commercialisation. Access compliance and these IP milestones require separate checks. [bda_s6] Match the applicant and activity to the correct form. Genuine foreign sourcing needs its own analysis and does not automatically eliminate biodiversity compliance. [bda_ipr_forms]

Not established by retrieved sources: Applicant category, the link between the IP and the Indian-accessed resource/knowledge, and current NBA procedures must be confirmed. Applicant identity, the actual sourcing country, intended use and provider-country obligations have not been established.

**State intimation and exemptions: section 7**

Established by source: Section 7 requires persons outside s.3(2) to give prior intimation to the State Biodiversity Board for the covered commercial access. Its proviso includes codified traditional knowledge, cultivated medicinal plants/products and specified local/professional categories; s.7(2) makes the cultivated-medicinal-plant exemption conditional on a certificate of origin from the Biodiversity Management Committee, with s.7(3) addressing records and issue. (s.7(1) proviso, s.7(2)-(3); Amendment Act s.9, p.4) [bda_s7_exemption] The 2025 Rules amendment replaces Rule 19 from 1 November 2025 with the prescribed BMC record/application/certificate procedure using Forms 11, 11A and 12 for cultivated medicinal plants. (G.S.R.295(E), 6 May 2025; substituted r.19; Forms11,11A,12; effective1 November2025) [bda_origin_2025]

Inference/application: For the plants you describe as cultivated, verify cultivation and the prescribed BMC certificate of origin for each material; a supplier's description alone does not complete that condition. Apply section 7 only to the covered applicant/access route; this exemption does not itself settle separate IP duties. [bda_s7_exemption] The certificate route concerns documented cultivated medicinal plants; a cultivation assertion alone does not complete the prescribed certificate process. [bda_origin_2025]

Not established by retrieved sources: Whether a particular source qualifies, whether the required certificate exists, and the applicable procedure require confirmation. Availability of the relevant BMC records, the certificate for the actual material/quantity and implementation of the procedure require confirmation.

**Access and Benefit Sharing**

Established by source: The Act provides for fair and equitable benefit-sharing conditions in the relevant approval framework; s.21 addresses benefit-sharing determination and possible forms of sharing. (ss.6(2), 18(1)-(2), 19(3A), 21(1), 23(b), 7(2)-(3)) [bda_abs] The 2025 ABS Regulations replace the 2014 regulations and prescribe different access and IP-commercialisation benefit-sharing frameworks, including distinct provisions for own commercial use and licensing. (Notification F.No.NBA/Tech/EC/9/14/32, 29 April 2025; regs.4-5, 8-9, 11, 13) [bda_abs_2025]

Inference/application: ABS obligations can arise where the applicable access/IP approval framework is triggered; an exemption from one procedural step does not by itself decide all benefit-sharing obligations. [bda_abs] An access-related exemption or nil access rate cannot automatically be used to decide the separate IP-commercialisation liability. [bda_abs_2025]

Not established by retrieved sources: The applicable current regulations, calculation base/rate, recipients, exemptions and approval terms for this applicant/source require confirmation; no case-specific amount is established here. The applicable trigger, exemptions, calculation base, turnover, licensing receipts, traditional-knowledge factors and approval conditions are needed to determine a case-specific amount.

**Sourcing and origin records**

Established by source: Biological-resource access and commercial utilisation depend on the statutory definitions, resource and activity. (ss.2(a), 2(c), 2(ea), 2(f), 2(fa), 2(p)) [bda_scope] The cultivated medicinal-plant exemption in section 7 requires the prescribed BMC certificate of origin. (s.7(1) proviso, s.7(2)-(3); Amendment Act s.9, p.4) [bda_s7_exemption] The 2025 ABS Regulations' Form B specifies resource and sourcing particulars, including names, plant parts, quantities, access dates, wild/cultivated/trader/repository sources, geographical location and relevant supplier or traditional-knowledge particulars. (reg.5 and Form B; regs.11-13) [bda_sourcing] The 2025 Rules amendment replaces Rule 19 from 1 November 2025 with the prescribed BMC record/application/certificate procedure using Forms 11, 11A and 12 for cultivated medicinal plants. (G.S.R.295(E), 6 May 2025; substituted r.19; Forms11,11A,12; effective1 November2025) [bda_origin_2025] Section 10(4) addresses disclosure of source and geographical origin of biological material used in the invention. (s.10(4)(a)-(c); s.10(4)(d) proviso (ii)(D); ss.25(1)(j), 64(1)(p)) [patents_specification] Rule 157A requires the specified annual raw-material record in Schedule TA, submitted to the State Drug Licensing Authority and National Medicinal Plants Board or its nominee by 30 June of the following financial year. Rules 158 and 160 require relevant manufacturing, testing and identification records. (rr.157A, 158(a), 160; Schedule TA) [dc_sourcing_records] Rule 18 prescribes Form 10 for the covered use in India of resources or knowledge obtained from a foreign country. (G.S.R.665(E), 22 October2024; rr.16,18; Forms7-10) [bda_ipr_forms]

[bda_s7_exemption] Maintain a separate provenance record for each plant/material and supply batch, distinguishing wild collection from cultivation even when one supplier supplies both. Record the applicable Form B particulars; linking invoices and batch records is a practical way to support the claimed provenance. [bda_sourcing] The certificate route concerns documented cultivated medicinal plants; a cultivation assertion alone does not complete the prescribed certificate process. [bda_origin_2025] Give the patent drafter substantiated biological-material provenance. [patents_specification] ASU manufacturing records are separate from biodiversity certificates and agreements; one document does not automatically satisfy every record-keeping duty. [dc_sourcing_records] Foreign sourcing needs a separate provider-country and Indian declaration analysis. [bda_ipr_forms]

Not established by retrieved sources: The material, access dates, origin and activity remain unverified. The certificate and relevant cultivation records have not been supplied. Which filings and fields apply to this activity, and whether the suppliers' records substantiate the claims, remain unverified. Availability of the relevant BMC records, the certificate for the actual material/quantity and implementation of the procedure require confirmation. The actual source/geographical origin declarations and any applicable deposit requirements need review. The facility's licensing circumstances and completeness of the actual raw-material and testing records require review. The actual foreign source and provider-country obligations remain unverified.

**Manufacturing licence and regulatory evidence**

Established by source: The ASU provisions require the applicable manufacturing licence and compliance with its conditions; the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules establish the State Licensing Authority and the relevant licensing procedure. (s.33EEC(c); rr.152-154, 157) [dc_licensing] Rule 158B differentiates classical and patent/proprietary ASU medicines and prescribes the applicable evidence requirements for a manufacturing licence. (r.158B, especially II(B) and V) [dc_rule_158b] Schedule T sets GMP requirements for ASU manufacture, including premises, hygiene, equipment, quality control and documentation. (rr.155B, 157(1), 158; Schedule T) [dc_schedule_t]

[dc_rule_158b] An eligible ASU manufacturing operation needs the applicable Schedule T compliance as part of its licensing preparation. [dc_schedule_t]

Facility compliance, quality-control arrangements and product-specific documentation have not been assessed.

**Advertising and disease-treatment claims**

citations.title: SBB intimation exemptions and the cultivated-plant certificate requirement
citations.snippet: Section 7(1) requires persons outside s.3(2) to give prior intimation to the concerned State Biodiversity Board before accessing biological resources and associated knowledge for commercial utilisation, subject to the Act. Its proviso lists codified traditional knowledge, cultivated medicinal plants and their products, local people and communities including growers and cultivators, and vaids, hakims and registered AYUSH practitioners practising indigenous medicine as a profession for sustenance and livelihood. Under s.7(2), the cultivated medicinal plant exemption is available only if a certificate of origin is obtained from the Biodiversity Management Committee in the prescribed manner; s.7(3) addresses its issue from maintained records. This section-specific exemption should not be presented as a blanket waiver of all IP-related or benefit-sharing obligations; check the applicable applicant, material, sourcing and regulatory conditions.

citations.statute: Biological Diversity Act, 2002, as amended in 2023
citations.title: Biodiversity scope depends on material, activity and actual source
citations.snippet: Access includes collecting, procuring or possessing biological resources occurring in or obtained from India or associated traditional knowledge for research, bio-survey or commercial use. Biological resources include plants, genetic material and derivatives, excluding value-added products; s.2(p) defines value-added products by unrecognisable and physically inseparable plant/animal portions or extracts. Commercial utilisation expressly includes drugs and extracts. Codified traditional knowledge is knowledge derived from First Schedule authoritative books. A medicinal product label, Indian plant species name, purchase from a trader, or final-product processing alone does not establish the access history or all exemptions; assess the actual material and sourcing chain.

citations.title: NBA IP and foreign-source declarations under the 2024 rules
citations.snippet: Rule16 provides Form7 for s.3(2) persons seeking NBA approval before IP grant; Form8 registration before grant for s.7 persons; and Form9 prior approval for commercialisation by s.7 persons. Rule18 requires a Form10 declaration from persons intending to use in India biological resources or associated traditional knowledge obtained from a foreign country for research, commerce or obtaining IP, under s.36A. Thus genuinely foreign sourcing has its own provider-country/Indian declaration analysis and is not proof that biodiversity compliance disappears. citations.title: Cultivated medicinal-plant certificate procedure after November 2025

Applications for a certificate of origin under s.7(2) are made to the BMC with the prescribed fee in Form11A on the portal; the certificate is generated as Form12 from those records. Form11 includes plant names, botanical/common names, cultivation period and approximate annual quantity; Form11A identifies applicant, State, district, BMC, plant and quantity. citations.statute: EU Directive 2004/24/EC (Traditional Herbal Medicinal Products Directive) + COM(2008)584
citations.title: EU traditional-use herbal registration and the Ayurveda market-access barrier
citations.snippet: Directive 2004/24/EC created a SIMPLIFIED traditional-use registration for herbal medicinal products in the EU, requiring evidence of at least 30 years of medicinal use, including at least 15 years within the EU, without new safety/efficacy clinical trials. The 2008 Commission report COM(2008)584 declined to extend the scheme to regulate whole traditional medical SYSTEMS as such (Ayurveda/TCM), calling that 'not appropriate for a global regulation of such medical practices' — but noted individual products can still qualify. The real product-level barrier for Ayurvedic products is the 15-years-in-EU use requirement, which the report acknowledges can prevent EU market access for third-country products.

citations.title: Definition of a patent or proprietary medicine (ASU)
citations.snippet: Section 3(h)(i) defines patent or proprietary medicines in the ASU systems as formulations containing only ingredients mentioned in formulae in the First Schedule authoritative books, while excluding parenteral medicines and formulations themselves included in those books. An original four-plant formulation potentially fits this category only if all ingredients satisfy that textual ingredient test and it is non-parenteral. The statutory word patent does not mean an invention patent has been granted or is required.
citations.review_note: Checked in official CDSCO compilation amended through 31 December 2016, pp.6 and 8. Classification depends on complete ingredients, their textual references, intended use and route, not a product label or patent grant.

citations.title: Biodiversity sourcing evidence and associated knowledge
citations.snippet: FormB for s.7 prior intimation asks for applicant details and annual turnover; state-wise biological-resource common and scientific names, plant parts, quantities, access dates, source type (wild/cultivated/institution/repository/trader/market), geographical location, and trader/institution contacts or repository passport/origin data. It also asks whether associated knowledge is oral/documented and identifies the knowledge holder and address. Reg13 sets agreement content including resource details, intended uses, IP conditions and benefit sharing. A practical sourcing dossier should preserve invoices/batch links, the applicable approvals/agreements, origin certificates and provider records needed to substantiate these declared facts; not every such supporting document is a universally named statutory certificate.
citations.review_note: Read official ABS2025 FormB pp23-24 and regs11-13 pp20-21. Invoice/batch links are a practical evidence recommendation, distinguished from expressly listed FormB fields.

citations.section: ss.3(1)-(2); amendment s.5; Biological Diversity Rules, 2024 r.13
citations.title: Section 3 applicant status and prior NBA access approval
citations.snippet: Section 3 requires previous NBA approval for obtaining covered biological resources occurring in India or associated knowledge for research, commercial utilisation or bio-survey/bio-utilisation by persons in s.3(2). Those categories are non-citizens; Indian citizens who are non-residents under Income-tax Act s.2(30); entities not incorporated/registered in India; and Indian-incorporated/registered entities controlled by a foreigner within Companies Act s.2(27). The 2023 amendment replaced the older foreign participation test with foreign control. Indian incorporation by itself does not settle the category. Rule13 uses Form1 for research/bio-survey and Form2 for commercial utilisation. Company control, citizenship/residence, purpose and actual access must be established.

citations.statute: Biological Diversity Act, 2002, as amended by Act 10 of 2023
citations.section: s.6(1), s.6(1A), s.6(1B); Amendment Act s.8, pp.3-4
citations.title: Biodiversity IP duties: approval, registration and commercialisation depend on applicant category
citations.snippet: For IP based on research or information on a biological resource accessed from India (including resources deposited in repositories outside India), or associated traditional knowledge, the 2023 amendment distinguishes applicant categories. Under s.6(1), persons or entities covered by s.3(2) require NBA approval before grant of the intellectual property right. Under s.6(1A), persons covered by s.7 require NBA registration before grant. Under s.6(1B), such s.7 persons who obtain the IP right require prior NBA approval at the time of commercialisation. These are not a single, uniform approval-before-filing rule for every applicant. Establish the applicant category and check current NBA procedures before acting.

citations.statute: Biological Diversity (Access to Biological Resources and Knowledge Associated thereto and Fair and Equitable Sharing of Benefits) Regulations, 2025
citations.title: 2025 ABS framework: separate access and IP-commercialisation routes
citations.snippet: The 2025 Regulations supersede the2014 regulations, saving things previously done or omitted. Regulations4(1) and5(7) set commercial-access benefit-sharing tables by annual turnover: up to Rs5crore nil; above5 to50crore 0.2%; above50 to250crore 0.4%; above250crore 0.6% of annual gross ex-factory sale price of the product excluding Government taxes. Special provisions apply to high-value/conservation/threatened resources, and regs4(2)/5(9) require annual FormA statements for turnover above Rs1crore. Regulations8 and9 address IP commercialisation for s.3 and s.7 persons respectively: case-specific own-use benefit sharing up to1%, and licensing/assignment sharing up to5% of fees and up to5% of annual royalties, with the stated traditional-knowledge uplift and other conditions. Their explanations provide that during IP existence, covered access benefits are shared only under the relevant IP-commercialisation regulation. Reg11 supplies case-specific determination factors. Reg5 exemptions depend on their statutory/notification conditions, including notified mixed cultivated/non-cultivated products; they cannot be presumed for every herbal medicine. These are potential frameworks, not a calculation of the user's liability.

citations.statute: The Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Drugs Rules, 1945
citations.title: State licensing is required for ASU manufacture for sale
citations.snippet: Section 33EEC(c) prohibits manufacture for sale or distribution of ASU drugs except under and in accordance with a licence issued by the prescribed authority, subject to the section's exceptions. Rule 152 provides for State-appointed licensing authorities; rules 153-154 govern the manufacturing application and licence (Form 24D and Form 25D). Rule 157 specifies licence conditions. An ordinary company commercial launch should establish the competent State/UT ASU licensing authority, manufacturing premises and applicable licence conditions. A proprietary ASU category does not automatically become a CDSCO new drug merely because its formula is novel.

citations.title: Licensing of ASU drugs — classical vs patent/proprietary
citations.snippet: Rule 158B distinguishes ASU classical, proprietary and medicinal-plant-extract licensing categories and their evidence requirements. In II(B), the proprietary-medicine row with textual ingredients/rationale specifies published literature of ingredients and a pilot study under the relevant ASU protocol; the Schedule E(1) ingredient row requires safety study and effectiveness evidence. Part V distinguishes aqueous, hydro-alcoholic and other extracts, with different safety/effectiveness requirements. Novel extraction technique, indications and Schedule E(1) status must therefore be mapped to the correct row rather than assuming one universal clinical-trial requirement.

citations.statute: Biological Diversity Act, 2002, as amended in 2023
citations.title: NBA, SBB and BMC roles and benefit-sharing duties
citations.snippet: NBA regulates activities under sections3,4 and6 and determines benefit sharing when granting approvals. Section21(1) requires fair and equitable sharing of benefits from accessed biological resources, derivatives, innovations and related knowledge through mutually agreed terms between the applicant and the BMC represented by NBA. Section6(2) permits benefit-sharing fees, royalties or other financial-sharing conditions with IP approval. State Biodiversity Boards regulate s.7 activities under s.23(b); BMCs maintain cultivation records and issue origin certificates under s.7(2)-(3). citations.statute: The Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 — Rule 170 (omission saga)
citations.title: Rule 170: dated timeline of omission and Supreme Court orders
citations.snippet: Rule 170 required prior approval of advertisements of Ayurvedic/Siddha/Unani drugs by the State Licensing Authority. Timeline: the AYUSH Ministry directed non-enforcement (Aug 2023); Rule 170 was OMITTED by the Drugs (Fourth Amendment) Rules 2024 (G.S.R. 360(E), effective 01 Jul 2024); the Supreme Court STAYED that omission on 27 Aug 2024 during the IMA/Patanjali contempt case; and on 11 Aug 2025 the Supreme Court VACATED that stay and disposed of the IMA petition. The dossier reports that the omission consequently stood after that order, while ASU advertising remained subject to the DMR Act 1954. This is a dated research timeline, not confirmation of the rule's present legal status; later orders and notifications must be checked.

citations.title: Definition of an Ayurvedic/Siddha/Unani (ASU) drug
citations.snippet: Section 3(a) defines Ayurvedic, Siddha or Unani drugs to include all medicines intended for internal or external use for or in the diagnosis, treatment, mitigation or prevention of disease or disorder in human beings or animals, and manufactured exclusively in accordance with the formulae described in the authoritative books of Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani Tibb systems specified in the First Schedule. This 'exclusively per First-Schedule formula' test is what marks a CLASSICAL medicine.

citations.title: Good Manufacturing Practices for ASU drugs
citations.snippet: Schedule T prescribes the Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP) for Ayurvedic, Siddha and Unani drug manufacturing units — covering factory premises, hygiene, machinery, quality control and documentation. A manufacturing licence for classical or patent/proprietary ASU drugs requires compliance with Schedule T.

citations.statute: The Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954
citations.title: Prohibition of objectionable advertisements
citations.snippet: The DMR Act prohibits advertisements that claim to diagnose, cure or prevent the diseases/conditions listed in its Schedule, and prohibits misleading advertisements of drugs (including ASU medicines). It is the principal control on disease-claim advertising for Ayurvedic products and was central to the Patanjali/IMA misleading-advertisements litigation.

citations.title: Patent disclosure and biological source/origin
citations.snippet: A complete specification must fully and particularly describe the invention and its operation or use and method of performance, disclose the best method known to the applicant for which protection is claimed, and define the scope through claims. The biological-material provision requires disclosure of source and geographical origin when used in an invention. Failure to disclose, or wrong disclosure of, source or geographical origin is a ground of opposition under s.25(1)(j) and revocation under s.64(1)(p). Required enabling details and the best method cannot simply be withheld from a patent specification as trade secrets.

citations.title: Manufacturing and raw-material records

Rule 158(a) requires manufacturing and test records for raw materials and finished products; rule 160 requires identification and available genuineness tests and their records. These records are distinct from biodiversity origin certificates and ABS agreements.

**Earlier facts withdrawn by your correction**

- “We plan an Ayurvedic oral syrup containing vasaka and tulsi.”
- “India label: 'Ayurvedic proprietary medicine'; Germany label: 'traditional herbal medicine'; US label: 'dietary supplement'.”
- “Our website will say 'cures bronchitis'.”
- “All herbs are cultivated in India and bought from traders; our company has a German majority shareholder.”
- “We have not fixed dosage, proved a history of medicinal use in Europe, or checked US ingredient notification history.”

**Facts supplied by you (unverified)**

- “We now make only an externally applied Ayurvedic hair oil containing bhringraj and sesame oil, not vasaka or tulsi.”
- “We sell only in India, with no Germany or US exports.”
- “The company is wholly Indian-owned.”
- “All plants are grown on our own farm.”
- “The only claim is 'hair conditioning'; there is no disease-treatment claim.”
- “No comparison with authoritative Ayurvedic texts has been completed.”

**Facts still needed and conditional outcomes**

- **What are the complete ingredients and quantities, their authoritative-text references, the exact formula, dosage form, route and intended claims? Studying classical texts alone does not supply those details.** Inference/application: If the complete formulation and manufacture match a First-Schedule authoritative formula, assess the classical route; if they do not, that classical test is not met (s.3(a)) [dc_3a] A non-classical formulation may fit the proprietary route only if all ingredients meet its book-based test and administration is non-parenteral; neither a new brand nor company development establishes this (s.3(h)(i)) [dc_3h]
- **What evidence verifies the stated ownership/control and establishes the actual applicant's statutory category?** Inference/application: You supplied these applicant/entity assertions: “The company is wholly Indian-owned.” Verify the actual applicant's incorporation and control, and citizenship/residence where applicable, against section 3(2). Stated Indian ownership or a foreign shareholder alone does not settle that statutory category. Apply prior NBA approval only to the covered applicant and access purpose; company share ownership does not determine ownership of IP. (ss.3(1)-(2); amendment s.5; Biological Diversity Rules, 2024 r.13) [bda_s3] If the applicant falls within section 3(2), assess prior NBA approval for covered access; an Indian manufacturing address does not settle citizenship, residence or foreign control (ss.3(1)-(2); amendment s.5; Biological Diversity Rules, 2024 r.13) [bda_s3] For a person outside section 3(2), assess section 7 prior SBB intimation and its actual exemptions for covered commercial access (s.7(1) proviso, s.7(2)-(3); Amendment Act s.9, p.4) [bda_s7_exemption] The same applicant distinction changes the IP milestone: NBA approval before grant for section 3(2) persons, versus pre-grant registration and applicable commercialisation approval for section 7 persons (s.6(1), s.6(1A), s.6(1B); Amendment Act s.8, pp.3-4) [bda_s6]

**Classical or proprietary medicine**

Established by source: The classical ASU definition requires manufacture exclusively according to formulae in the authoritative books listed in the First Schedule. (s.3(a)) [dc_3a] An ASU patent or proprietary medicine must contain only ingredients mentioned in formulae in First-Schedule authoritative books; the formulation itself must not be included there, and parenteral medicines are excluded. (s.3(h)(i)) [dc_3h]

Inference/application: Classical status remains unresolved: compare the complete formula and manufacture with a First-Schedule formula. Developing a combination yourself or studying classical texts does not establish either a match or its absence. [dc_3a] The proprietary category is conditional on every ingredient meeting the First-Schedule book test, the formulation itself being absent from those formulae, and a non-parenteral route. Calling the product new or proprietary does not verify those facts or establish patentability. [dc_3h]

Not established by retrieved sources: The exact formula and its comparison with the relevant authoritative books have not been verified. The supplied product ingredients or route are unverified. The complete ingredient list, ingredient-by-ingredient authoritative-book references, formulation comparison and exact administration route must establish every condition of this definition.

**Biodiversity access: section 3 and applicant status**

Established by source: Section 3 requires prior NBA approval for the specified access purposes by persons within s.3(2), which distinguishes non-citizens, the specified non-resident citizens and covered foreign/foreign-controlled entities. (ss.3(1)-(2); amendment s.5; Biological Diversity Rules, 2024 r.13) [bda_s3] The Biological Diversity Act defines biological resources and commercial utilisation and includes specific exclusions; applicability depends on the resource, associated knowledge and activity. (ss.2(a), 2(c), 2(ea), 2(f), 2(fa), 2(p)) [bda_scope]

Inference/application: You supplied these applicant/entity assertions: “The company is wholly Indian-owned.” Verify the actual applicant's incorporation and control, and citizenship/residence where applicable, against section 3(2). Stated Indian ownership or a foreign shareholder alone does not settle that statutory category. Apply prior NBA approval only to the covered applicant and access purpose; company share ownership does not determine ownership of IP. [bda_s3] The Indian identity or name of a plant alone does not settle the access route. The material's actual source and whether the accessed item falls within the statutory definitions matter. [bda_scope]

Not established by retrieved sources: Ownership/control assertions have been supplied but not verified. Confirm the actual applicant and documentary incorporation/control or citizenship/residence details, the access purpose and the material, before deciding the statutory applicant category. Actual sourcing, material type, date/purpose of access and any relevant exemption remain to be verified.

**Biodiversity duties for IP: section 6**

Established by source: For IP based on research/information on a biological resource accessed from India (including deposits in repositories outside India), or associated traditional knowledge, s.6(1) requires s.3(2) persons to obtain NBA approval before grant. Section 6(1A) requires NBA registration by s.7 persons before grant; under s.6(1B), those s.7 persons obtaining the IP right need prior NBA approval at commercialisation. (s.6(1), s.6(1A), s.6(1B); Amendment Act s.8, pp.3-4) [bda_s6] Rule 16 of the 2024 Rules prescribes Form 7 for s.3(2) IP approval, Form 8 for s.7 pre-grant registration and Form 9 for s.7 commercialisation approval. Rule 18 prescribes Form 10 for the covered use in India of resources or associated knowledge obtained from a foreign country. (G.S.R.665(E), 22 October2024; rr.16,18; Forms7-10) [bda_ipr_forms]

Inference/application: If the IP is based on the covered Indian-accessed resource or associated knowledge, identify the applicant category: section 3(2) persons need NBA approval before grant; section 7 persons need NBA registration before grant and, if they obtain the IP right, prior NBA approval at commercialisation. Access compliance and these IP milestones require separate checks. [bda_s6] Match the applicant and activity to the correct form. Genuine foreign sourcing needs its own analysis and does not automatically eliminate biodiversity compliance. [bda_ipr_forms]

Not established by retrieved sources: Applicant category, the link between the IP and the Indian-accessed resource/knowledge, and current NBA procedures must be confirmed. Applicant identity, the actual sourcing country, intended use and provider-country obligations have not been established.

Established by source: Section 7 requires persons outside s.3(2) to give prior intimation to the State Biodiversity Board for the covered commercial access. Its proviso includes codified traditional knowledge, cultivated medicinal plants/products and specified local/professional categories; s.7(2) makes the cultivated-medicinal-plant exemption conditional on a certificate of origin from the Biodiversity Management Committee, with s.7(3) addressing records and issue. Apply section 7 only to the covered applicant/access route; this exemption does not itself settle separate IP duties. [bda_s7_exemption] The certificate route concerns documented cultivated medicinal plants; a cultivation assertion alone does not complete the prescribed certificate process. [bda_origin_2025]

citations.snippet: Access includes collecting, procuring or possessing biological resources occurring in or obtained from India or associated traditional knowledge for research, bio-survey or commercial use. citations.snippet: Rule 158B distinguishes ASU classical, proprietary and medicinal-plant-extract licensing categories and their evidence requirements. citations.title: 2025 ABS framework: separate access and IP-commercialisation routes
citations.snippet: The 2025 Regulations supersede the2014 regulations, saving things previously done or omitted. Regulations4(1) and5(7) set commercial-access benefit-sharing tables by annual turnover: up to Rs5crore nil; above5 to50crore 0.2%; above50 to250crore 0.4%; above250crore 0.6% of annual gross ex-factory sale price of the product excluding Government taxes. Special provisions apply to high-value/conservation/threatened resources, and regs4(2)/5(9) require annual FormA statements for turnover above Rs1crore. Regulations8 and9 address IP commercialisation for s.3 and s.7 persons respectively: case-specific own-use benefit sharing up to1%, and licensing/assignment sharing up to5% of fees and up to5% of annual royalties, with the stated traditional-knowledge uplift and other conditions. Their explanations provide that during IP existence, covered access benefits are shared only under the relevant IP-commercialisation regulation. Reg11 supplies case-specific determination factors. Reg5 exemptions depend on their statutory/notification conditions, including notified mixed cultivated/non-cultivated products; they cannot be presumed for every herbal medicine. These are potential frameworks, not a calculation of the user's liability.

**Facts still needed and conditional outcomes**

- **What precise formulation or process features would be claimed, and what prior-art comparison and experimental data support the claimed technical contribution?** Inference/application: Insufficient evidence in retrieved sources to determine inventorship, initial ownership or the effect of employment, university, funding and assignment terms. Record each contributor's precise technical/creative contribution separately from the documents claiming or transferring title. The supplied employee, university or designer relationship does not establish the company's title in this answer; obtain the relevant ownership provisions and agreements before deciding. Patentability rules do not answer this question.

**Patent eligibility for the formulation and process**

Established by source: A patentable invention must be a new product or process involving an inventive step and capable of industrial application; the Act separately defines inventive step and new invention. (ss.2(1)(j), 2(1)(ja), 2(1)(l)) [patents_invention] Section 48 provides the specified exclusive rights for patented products and processes in India; ss.73–74 identify the Controller of Patents and Patent Office. (ss.48, 73-74) [patents_rights]

Inference/application: You describe a separate process: “We also have a separate extraction process that might be new, but no prior-art search is complete.”. Assess its actual claims independently for novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability; saying the process might be new, or reporting an incomplete prior-art search, does not establish those tests. The conclusions on a salt or mixture do not decide this separate process. [patents_invention] A patent may protect qualifying product/process claims, but does not itself establish regulatory permission to sell or freedom to operate against other patents. [patents_rights]

Not established by retrieved sources: No prior-art search, claim analysis or experimental evidence has established that this particular invention satisfies those tests. The scope of proposed claims, third-party rights and regulatory clearance require separate assessments.

**Patent exclusions**

Established by source: Traditional knowledge, and aggregation or duplication of known properties of traditionally known components, are excluded from inventions by s.3(p).
